content:
Short answer

The best open source LLMs to run locally depend mainly on your VRAM. As a rule of thumb at 4-bit quantization, a model needs roughly 0.55–0.65 GB per billion parameters plus room for context. With 8 GB you can run strong 7–8B models; 12–16 GB handles 12–14B models; 24 GB (RTX 3090/4090) runs 27–32B models well; 32 GB (RTX 5090) adds headroom for longer context; and 48–96 GB+ opens up 70B dense models and mid-size mixture-of-experts models. Leading open-weight families include Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek, Gemma, Mistral, gpt-oss, Phi, GLM and Kimi. New versions arrive every few months, so always check for the latest release in each family.

How to choose: the VRAM rule

Model size in memory ≈ parameters × bytes per weight, plus the KV cache for your context length.

Use our VRAM calculator for exact numbers, and see LLM quantization explained.

Best models by VRAM tier

Model names below are families and representative sizes; pick the newest version available in each family.

8 GB VRAM (RTX 3060 Ti, 4060, 5060)

At 4-bit, an 8B model uses about 5 GB, leaving room for several thousand tokens of context.

12–16 GB VRAM (RTX 3060 12 GB, 4060 Ti 16 GB, 5060 Ti 16 GB, 5070 Ti)

24 GB VRAM (RTX 3090, RTX 4090)

This is the sweet spot for local AI.

A 32B model at 4-bit uses about 19–20 GB, leaving a few GB for context.

32 GB VRAM (RTX 5090)

Run the same 27–32B models with higher precision (5–6 bit) or much longer context, or squeeze larger MoE models with partial CPU offload. See RTX 5090 vs RTX 4090 for AI.

48–96 GB VRAM (2 × 24 GB, RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, Macs with large unified memory)

A 70B model at 4-bit needs about 40–43 GB, which fits on two 24 GB GPUs. See multi-GPU local LLM setup.

128 GB+ (multi-GPU rigs, high-memory Macs, servers)

The largest open-weight models, such as DeepSeek V3/R1-class, Qwen's largest MoE models, Kimi K2-class and GLM's flagship models, have hundreds of billions to around a trillion total parameters. Running them locally needs very large memory, aggressive quantization or CPU offload, and is best suited to enthusiasts with workstation or server hardware. For most people, renting cloud GPUs is more practical; see the GPU cloud price tracker.

Best picks by use case

Dense vs mixture-of-experts models locally

Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have many total parameters but activate only a fraction per token. Locally this means:

  • Memory: you still need room for all the weights (or offload some to system RAM).
  • Speed: generation is fast because only active parameters are read per token.
  • Offload-friendly: MoE models run surprisingly well with experts in system RAM using llama.cpp, making large models usable on modest GPUs with lots of RAM.

Tools to run them

See how to run an LLM locally and LLM inference engines compared.

Licences: "open" is not always the same

Some models use permissive licences (Apache 2.0 or MIT, for example many Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek, gpt-oss and Phi releases), while others use custom licences with usage conditions (for example Llama and Gemma). Check the licence on the model card before commercial use.

Tips for the best local results

1. Start with Q4_K_M (or equivalent), then move to Q5/Q6 if you have spare VRAM. 2. Keep the whole model on the GPU when possible; offloading to CPU slows generation a lot (except MoE expert offload). 3. Don't max out context unless needed: long contexts use a lot of memory. 4. Use the correct chat template; most tools handle this automatically. 5. Benchmark on your own tasks, not just leaderboards. See LLM benchmarks.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best LLM for a 24 GB GPU?

A current 27–32B model from the Qwen, Gemma or Mistral families at 4–5 bit quantization, or a ~30B MoE model for faster responses.

Can I run a 70B model on one GPU?

Only with 48 GB or more of VRAM at 4-bit, or with heavy quantization or CPU offload on 24–32 GB, which is slower.

Are open source LLMs as good as ChatGPT?

The best open-weight models are competitive with leading closed models on many tasks, though the largest frontier closed models usually stay ahead on the hardest problems. Smaller local models trade some quality for privacy and zero per-token cost.

Which open model is best for coding locally?

Coder-tuned models in the Qwen, DeepSeek and GLM families are popular choices; pick the largest that fits your VRAM with room for context.

Short answer

A small number of organisations are openly working toward superintelligence. The main companies building superintelligence are OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta Superintelligence Labs and xAI in the United States, the research-only Safe Superintelligence Inc., Microsoft's in-house superintelligence team, and Chinese labs such as DeepSeek and Alibaba's Qwen team. They differ in openness, business model and safety philosophy, but share three ingredients: frontier talent, enormous compute and the capital to buy it. This guide reflects public information as of late 2026; the landscape changes quickly.

How to read this guide

Company strategies, products and partnerships change often. Treat this as a snapshot of publicly stated goals and approaches, not a ranking of who will "win". For why this race matters strategically, see superintelligence geopolitics; for its history, see the history of superintelligence.

The main players at a glance

OpenAI

Founded in 2015 as a non-profit to ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, OpenAI created ChatGPT, the GPT model series and the first widely used reasoning models. In early 2025, its CEO wrote that the company was confident it knew how to build AGI and was beginning to turn its aim toward superintelligence. OpenAI has pursued very large compute partnerships for new data centers. Its safety approach includes a preparedness framework for evaluating dangerous capabilities and research on scalable oversight and reasoning-trace monitoring. Critics, including former employees, have argued that commercial pressure has at times outpaced safety; OpenAI says it balances both.

Google DeepMind

Formed by merging DeepMind and Google Brain in 2023, Google DeepMind combines one of the deepest research benches with Google's custom TPUs, data and products. It produced AlphaGo, AlphaFold (recognised with the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for Demis Hassabis and John Jumper), the Gemini models and AlphaEvolve. Its leadership emphasises AI's potential to accelerate science, see AI scientists and discovery, and it publishes a Frontier Safety Framework with capability thresholds. Owning its chips gives it unusual control over compute costs.

Anthropic

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers, Anthropic positions safety as central to its mission while building frontier Claude models. It introduced a Responsible Scaling Policy tying safeguards to capability levels, and it is a leader in interpretability research and in publishing studies of risky model behaviours such as alignment faking. Its CEO's 2024 essay *Machines of Loving Grace* described how powerful AI could compress decades of scientific progress into years. Anthropic argues that safety-focused labs need to be at the frontier to influence how powerful AI is built.

Meta Superintelligence Labs

In mid-2025 Meta reorganised its AI work into Meta Superintelligence Labs, recruiting prominent researchers and leaders, and its CEO described a vision of "personal superintelligence" available to everyone. Meta has a history of releasing open-weight Llama models and is building some of the largest AI data centers in the world. How open its most capable future models will be has been a subject of debate.

xAI

Founded by Elon Musk in 2023, xAI builds the Grok models and has assembled very large GPU clusters at speed. Musk was an early voice warning about AI risk and co-founded OpenAI before leaving. xAI emphasises rapid scaling and integration with the X platform.

Safe Superintelligence Inc. (SSI)

Co-founded in 2024 by Ilya Sutskever, OpenAI's former chief scientist, SSI says it will pursue safe superintelligence "in a straight shot", with no products until it gets there. It has raised large funding rounds at high valuations without releasing a model. Details of its technical approach are not public. Read our full profile: Safe Superintelligence Inc. explained.

Microsoft AI

Microsoft is OpenAI's largest backer and cloud partner, and also builds its own models. In late 2025 its AI division announced a superintelligence team focused on what it called "humanist superintelligence": highly capable AI designed to remain under human control and serve specific human goals, such as medical diagnosis, rather than open-ended autonomy.

Chinese labs

  • DeepSeek shocked markets in January 2025 with DeepSeek-R1, a reasoning model trained efficiently and released with open weights. Its research on mixture of experts and efficient attention (MLA) has been influential.
  • Alibaba develops the widely used open Qwen models and has described a roadmap toward artificial superintelligence, backed by major cloud investment.
  • Other labs, including Moonshot AI, Zhipu and ByteDance, release strong models. Export controls on advanced chips push Chinese labs toward efficiency. See superintelligence geopolitics.

Other notable players

  • Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati.
  • Mistral AI in Europe, focused on efficient open and commercial models.
  • NVIDIA, which supplies most of the compute and increasingly builds models and research of its own.
  • Academic and non-profit safety organisations, such as METR, Apollo Research, Redwood Research and the UK AI Security Institute, which evaluate frontier systems.

What separates the leaders

See how much compute superintelligence needs for the hardware side.

Comparing safety approaches

Critics argue that all companies face competitive pressure to move fast, which is why many call for binding regulation and international coordination. See the superintelligence control problem and the superintelligence statement.

What to watch

1. Compute announcements: gigawatt campuses and new chip orders. 2. Model capability jumps: especially in autonomous agents and AI-driven research. 3. Safety disclosures: system cards, dangerous-capability evaluations and incident reports. 4. Talent moves: key researchers switching labs often signal strategic shifts. 5. Policy: regulation, export controls and international agreements that constrain or shape the race.

Frequently asked questions

Which company is closest to superintelligence?

No one knows. Leadership changes with each model release, and the most capable systems may exist inside labs before public release. Benchmarks give partial signals; see AI benchmarks explained.

Is anyone building superintelligence openly?

Some labs release open-weight models, but none has published a complete open path to superintelligence. Openness is debated: it aids research and accountability but makes misuse harder to prevent.

Why are companies spending so much on superintelligence?

They believe whoever leads could capture enormous economic value and influence. See the economics of superintelligence.

Are governments building superintelligence?

Governments mainly fund research, compute and safety institutes, and partner with companies. Some analysts expect much deeper government involvement as capabilities grow.

content:
Short answer

GPU power consumption for AI depends on the card and the workload. High-end consumer GPUs draw up to 350 W (RTX 3090), 450 W (RTX 4090) and 575 W (RTX 5090) at full load, while data center GPUs draw 700 W (H100 SXM) to around 1,000 W (B200). Local LLM chat usually uses far less than maximum power because the GPU is idle between requests and token generation is memory-bound. To estimate cost: watts × hours ÷ 1,000 × your electricity price per kWh. For example, a 450 W load for 4 hours a day at $0.15/kWh costs about $0.27 a day. Setting a power limit of 70–80% often cuts consumption substantially with only a small loss in AI speed.

Typical GPU power figures

Idle figures vary with drivers, monitors and settings. Your whole PC also draws power: CPU, RAM, storage and fans typically add 80–200 W under load.

How much power do AI workloads really use?

How to calculate your electricity cost

Cost = (watts ÷ 1,000) × hours × price per kWh

1. Estimate total system power under your workload (GPU + rest of PC). A wall power meter gives the most accurate number. 2. Estimate hours per day at that load. 3. Look up your electricity price per kWh on your bill.

Worked examples (using $0.15/kWh)

Multiply by your actual tariff: at $0.30/kWh, costs double; at $0.08/kWh, they roughly halve. In regions with high electricity prices, power costs can be a significant part of local AI.

Local vs cloud: when does electricity tip the balance?

Running locally means paying for hardware plus electricity; renting means paying per hour. Consumer GPUs rent cheaply on marketplaces: our GPU cloud price tracker recently listed RTX 4090s from about $0.26/hour and RTX 5090s from about $0.29/hour. If you use a GPU only a few hours a week, renting can be cheaper than buying once electricity and hardware cost are included. For daily heavy use, owning usually wins. See rent vs buy a GPU.

How to reduce GPU power consumption

1. Set a power limit

Many AI workloads lose only a little speed when power is capped, because performance per watt is highest below maximum power.

# Linux / Windows (admin): set a 350 W limit on GPU 0
nvidia-smi -i 0 -pl 350

Test your own workload: a 70–80% limit often reduces power and heat considerably with a modest speed loss, especially for memory-bound LLM inference.

2. Undervolt

Tools such as MSI Afterburner (Windows) let you run the GPU at lower voltage for the same clock, improving efficiency and reducing temperatures and noise.

3. Use quantized models

Smaller weights mean less data moved per token and often faster, more efficient inference. See LLM quantization.

4. Unload models when idle

Tools like Ollama unload models after a period of inactivity; shorter keep-alive settings reduce idle draw slightly.

5. Choose efficient hardware

Newer GPUs and Apple Silicon deliver more AI work per watt. A 16 GB RTX 5060 Ti is far more efficient than an older high-power card for small models.

6. Batch your work

Generating many images or processing many documents in one session uses the GPU more efficiently than many short sessions.

Heat, noise and safety

  • Every watt consumed becomes heat in your room. A 600–800 W system running for hours warms a small room noticeably.
  • Ensure good case airflow and room ventilation.
  • Use a quality power supply with headroom and properly seated power connectors. See how to build an AI workstation.

Data center scale

At data center scale, power is a defining constraint: an 8-GPU H100 server draws about 10 kW, and GB200 NVL72 racks around 120 kW. See how much energy AI uses and liquid cooling for AI data centers.

Frequently asked questions

How many watts does an RTX 4090 use for AI?

Up to about 450 W at full load. LLM chat often uses less on average; image generation and training run closer to the maximum.

Is running a local LLM expensive?

For typical personal use, electricity costs are usually a few dollars to a few tens of dollars per month, depending on usage and local prices.

Does power limiting hurt AI performance?

Moderately at most for many workloads. Memory-bound LLM inference is often barely affected by a reasonable power cap.

Is a Mac more energy-efficient for AI?

Yes. Apple Silicon uses much less power, though it is generally slower than high-end NVIDIA GPUs.

The H100 PCIe is a standard plug-in card (80 GB HBM2e, about 2.0 TB/s, 350 W, slower compute). The H100 NVL is a PCIe card with 94 GB and about 3.9 TB/s, designed for LLM inference in pairs. content:
Short answer

The NVIDIA H100 comes in three main versions. The H100 SXM is the full-power data center module (80 GB HBM3, about 3.35 TB/s, up to 700 W, 900 GB/s NVLink). The H100 PCIe is a standard plug-in card (80 GB HBM2e, about 2.0 TB/s, 350 W, slower compute). The H100 NVL is a PCIe card with 94 GB and about 3.9 TB/s, designed for LLM inference in pairs. In the H100 PCIe vs SXM choice, SXM is significantly faster for training and multi-GPU work; PCIe is cheaper and fine for single-GPU inference and experiments. Always check which version a cloud listing uses.

The three H100 versions

Figures are approximate dense values; sparse figures quoted by NVIDIA are about twice as high.

Why SXM is faster

1. Higher power limit: 700 W versus 350 W lets the chip run more units at higher clocks. 2. Faster memory: HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s versus HBM2e at 2.0 TB/s, about 68% more bandwidth. Bandwidth drives LLM token generation. See GPU memory bandwidth. 3. More active compute: the SXM version enables more streaming multiprocessors. 4. NVLink and NVSwitch: all 8 GPUs in an HGX server talk to each other at 900 GB/s each, far faster than PCIe Gen5 (about 64 GB/s per direction on x16). This matters for tensor parallelism and multi-GPU training. See NVLink and NVSwitch and distributed training.

Real-world performance differences

The H100 NVL narrows the gap for inference: its 94 GB and 3.9 TB/s make it attractive for serving large models in pairs, though it lacks the 8-way NVSwitch fabric of SXM systems.

Price differences

PCIe H100s are often listed cheaper per GPU-hour than SXM. On our GPU cloud price tracker in late November 2026, the lowest on-demand H100 was about $1.80/hour and the median about $3.92/hour, with configurations varying between providers. A low price may indicate a PCIe card; check before comparing.

Cost per result matters more than cost per hour. If SXM finishes a job 1.5× faster, it can be cheaper overall even at a higher hourly price. See H100 price and cheapest cloud GPU.

How to tell which H100 you are getting

  • Look for "SXM", "SXM5" or "HGX" in the instance description; these are SXM.
  • "PCIe" in the name means the plug-in card.
  • "NVL" indicates the 94 GB PCIe variant.
  • 8-GPU instances on hyperscalers (such as AWS P5, Google A3, Azure ND H100 v5) use SXM.
  • Run nvidia-smi after launching: the product name and power limit (700 W vs 350 W) reveal the version.
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total,power.limit --format=csv

Which should you choose?

If you need more memory, consider the H200 (141 GB) or B200 (180 GB). For older alternatives, see H100 vs A100.

Frequently asked questions

Is the H100 PCIe much slower than SXM?

For single-GPU, memory-bound inference, it can be roughly 30–40% slower in proportion to bandwidth; for multi-GPU training, the gap is larger because PCIe cards lack the NVSwitch fabric.

Can H100 PCIe cards use NVLink?

Yes, pairs of PCIe cards can be connected with an NVLink bridge, but not in the 8-way all-to-all NVSwitch configuration of SXM systems.

What does SXM mean?

SXM is NVIDIA's socketed module form factor for data center GPUs, mounted directly on a baseboard with higher power and NVLink connections.

Is the H100 NVL better than SXM?

For some inference workloads, its larger memory and higher bandwidth help. For multi-GPU training, SXM systems with NVSwitch are better.

What changes from Hopper to Blackwell

Performance in real workloads

Memory: what fits on one GPU

Power, cooling and deployment

How much faster is the B200 than the H200?

For dense BF16 and FP8 compute, roughly 2.3× on paper; memory bandwidth is about 1.7× higher. FP4 adds further gains. Real-world speed-ups vary by workload.

Is the H200 obsolete?

No. It remains widely deployed, well supported and cost-effective for many training and inference jobs.

Does the B200 need liquid cooling?

Not always. Some 8-GPU HGX B200 systems are air-cooled, but liquid cooling is common for dense deployments and required for rack-scale GB200 systems.

Which is better for inference?

For large-scale or FP4 inference, the B200. For smaller deployments where models fit easily, the H200 can be cheaper.

Good described an "intelligence explosion" in 1965; Vernor Vinge popularised the "Singularity" in 1993; and Nick Bostrom's 2014 book Superintelligence made the risks a mainstream research topic. Deep learning breakthroughs from 2012, the transformer in 2017 and ChatGPT in 2022 turned the idea from philosophy into an engineering goal. By 2024–2025, leading labs openly described superintelligence as their target, while hundreds of researchers signed statements warning about its risks.

Why the history matters

Today's debates about superintelligence repeat arguments first made decades ago: whether machines can surpass humans, whether self-improvement could run away, and whether such systems could be controlled. Knowing where these ideas came from helps separate genuinely new evidence from recycled speculation.

Era 1: The founders (1950–1970)

1950 – Turing asks "Can machines think?" In *Computing Machinery and Intelligence*, Alan Turing proposed the imitation game (the Turing test) and rebutted objections that machines could never think.

1951 – The first warning. In a lecture, Turing suggested that once machines began to think, they would soon outstrip human abilities, and at some stage we should expect them to take control.

1956 – The Dartmouth workshop. John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and Nathaniel Rochester coined "artificial intelligence" and predicted rapid progress.

1965 – The intelligence explosion. Statistician I. J. Good, who worked with Turing at Bletchley Park, wrote that an "ultraintelligent machine" could design even better machines, leading to an "intelligence explosion" that would leave human intelligence far behind. He called it "the last invention that man need ever make", provided the machine was docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control. See the intelligence explosion.

1960s – Early alarm. Norbert Wiener, founder of cybernetics, warned in 1960 that we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into a machine is the purpose we really desire, an early statement of the alignment problem.

Era 2: AI winters and science fiction (1970–1999)

  • 1970s and late 1980s – AI winters: funding collapsed after early promises failed. Superintelligence faded from serious research.
  • 1968 – 2001: A Space Odyssey gave the public HAL 9000, an AI whose conflicting goals turn deadly.
  • 1984 – The Terminator fixed the killer-robot image in popular culture, an image researchers still struggle against. See superintelligence myths.
  • 1988 – Hans Moravec's *Mind Children* predicted robots would surpass humans and noted that skills easy for humans can be hard for machines (Moravec's paradox).
  • 1993 – The Singularity. Mathematician and author Vernor Vinge's essay *The Coming Technological Singularity* argued that within 30 years we would have the means to create superhuman intelligence, after which the human era would end.
  • 1997 – Deep Blue beats Kasparov, showing machines could surpass the best humans in a domain once considered a pinnacle of intellect.

Era 3: The safety pioneers (2000–2014)

  • 2000: Eliezer Yudkowsky co-founded the Singularity Institute, later the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), one of the first organisations focused on making advanced AI safe.
  • 2005: Ray Kurzweil's *The Singularity Is Near* predicted human-level AI by 2029 and a Singularity around 2045, reaching a wide audience.
  • 2005: Nick Bostrom founded the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford, a centre for existential-risk research until it closed in 2024.
  • 2008: Steve Omohundro described the "basic AI drives" that goal-directed systems might develop. See orthogonality and instrumental convergence.
  • 2010: DeepMind was founded with the mission to "solve intelligence".
  • 2012: AlexNet's victory in the ImageNet contest, trained on two gaming GPUs, launched the deep learning era. See What is a GPU?.

Era 4: The book that changed the debate (2014–2017)

  • 2014: Nick Bostrom published *Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies*, laying out paths to SI, the control problem, and concepts such as the treacherous turn and the paperclip maximiser. Endorsements from Elon Musk and Bill Gates, and public concern from Stephen Hawking, brought the topic to mainstream attention. Read our guide to Bostrom's Superintelligence.
  • 2015: The Future of Life Institute's open letter on research priorities for robust and beneficial AI gathered thousands of signatures. OpenAI was founded as a non-profit to ensure artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.
  • 2016: AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol, a decade earlier than many experts expected. Researchers published *Concrete Problems in AI Safety*, turning safety into technical research.
  • 2017: Google researchers introduced the transformer, the architecture behind today's language models. See What is a transformer?. The Asilomar AI Principles were adopted at a major conference.

Era 5: Scaling and language models (2018–2022)

  • 2019: Stuart Russell's *Human Compatible* proposed rebuilding AI around uncertainty about human preferences. See the superintelligence control problem.
  • 2020: OpenAI's GPT-3 and the scaling laws paper showed capabilities improving predictably with compute. DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 solved much of the protein-folding problem.
  • 2021: Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI researchers with a focus on AI safety.
  • November 30, 2022: ChatGPT launched and reached an enormous audience within weeks, making advanced AI part of everyday life.

Era 6: Mainstream alarm and acceleration (2023–2024)

  • March 2023: GPT-4 launched. An open letter called for a six-month pause on training systems more powerful than GPT-4.
  • May 2023: Geoffrey Hinton left Google to speak freely about AI risks. The Center for AI Safety's one-sentence statement that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority was signed by hundreds of leading researchers and executives.
  • July 2023: OpenAI announced a "superalignment" team to solve the alignment of superintelligent systems within four years; the team was dissolved in 2024 after key departures.
  • November 2023: The UK hosted the first AI Safety Summit, producing the Bletchley Declaration.
  • 2024: Ilya Sutskever co-founded Safe Superintelligence Inc. with the sole goal of building safe SI. Kurzweil published *The Singularity Is Nearer*. Geoffrey Hinton and John Hopfield received the Nobel Prize in Physics for foundations of machine learning; Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold. OpenAI's o1 introduced reasoning models. The AI 2027 authors began work on a detailed fast-takeoff forecast.

Era 7: The open race for superintelligence (2025– )

  • January 2025: DeepSeek-R1 showed strong reasoning could be trained efficiently and released openly. OpenAI's CEO wrote that the company was beginning to turn its aim beyond AGI to superintelligence.
  • 2025: Meta created Meta Superintelligence Labs. Google DeepMind and OpenAI models reached gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad. AI systems such as AlphaEvolve began contributing original algorithmic discoveries.
  • 2025: Research found early signs of alignment faking and scheming in controlled tests of frontier models. See early warning signs in today's AI.
  • October 2025: The superintelligence statement called for prohibiting superintelligence development until it could be done safely and controllably with strong public support, signed by scientists, public figures and many others.
  • 2025–2026: Gigawatt-scale AI data center projects, new chip generations and national strategies made compute and geopolitics central to the story.

Timeline at a glance

Patterns across 75 years

1. Timelines were often wrong in both directions. Early pioneers expected human-level AI within a generation; later sceptics were surprised by Go, protein folding and language models. See when will AGI arrive?. 2. The core arguments were set early. Good's explosion, Wiener's goal problem and Turing's control worry anticipate today's debates. 3. Hardware drove the turning points. GPUs, then massive clusters, unlocked each new era. See the hardware road to SI. 4. Safety research grew from fringe to mainstream, but still trails capability investment by a wide margin. 5. Superintelligence moved from philosophy to corporate strategy, which changes the stakes of every unanswered question.

Frequently asked questions

Who first came up with the idea of superintelligence?

Alan Turing hinted at it in 1951, but I. J. Good's 1965 description of an intelligence explosion is usually treated as the first clear statement. Nick Bostrom popularised the term "superintelligence" in its modern sense.

What is the Singularity?

A hypothetical point when technological growth, driven by superhuman AI, becomes so fast that the future beyond it is unpredictable. Vernor Vinge popularised it in 1993 and Ray Kurzweil predicted it around 2045.

When did AI companies start aiming for superintelligence?

Several labs described AGI as their goal from their founding. From around 2024–2025, leading companies began naming superintelligence itself as an explicit objective. See which companies are building superintelligence.

  • Good, I. J., "Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine", *Advances in Computers* (1965)
  • Vinge, The Coming Technological Singularity (1993)
  • Bostrom, *Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies* (Oxford University Press, 2014)
  • Center for AI Safety, Statement on AI Risk (2023)
  • The Nobel Prize, Nobel Prize in Physics 2024

LABEL: EXPLAINER

META: Liquid cooling for AI data centers explained: why GPU racks outgrew air, direct-to-chip cold plates, immersion cooling, PUE, water use and costs.

content:
Short answer

Liquid cooling for AI data centers has become essential because AI hardware produces too much heat for air alone. A traditional server rack draws roughly 5–15 kW; an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack draws around 120 kW. Air cooling struggles beyond about 30–50 kW per rack. The main solution is direct-to-chip liquid cooling, where cold plates on GPUs and CPUs carry heat away in a liquid loop; immersion cooling submerges whole servers in non-conductive fluid. Liquid cooling allows denser racks, can improve energy efficiency, and is now a key factor in where the newest GPUs can be deployed.

Why AI broke air cooling

Heat removal scales with how much air you can push through a server. As chip power climbed, fans and air handlers hit physical limits:

Water carries heat thousands of times more effectively than the same volume of air. Once racks pass a few tens of kilowatts, liquid becomes the practical option. See what is an AI data center? and GB200 NVL72 explained.

The main liquid cooling methods

Key components

  • Cold plates: attached to hot chips, with micro-channels for coolant.
  • Coolant distribution unit (CDU): pumps coolant and exchanges heat between the rack loop and the facility water loop.
  • Manifolds and quick-disconnect fittings: connect servers to the loop without leaks.
  • Facility water loop and heat rejection: dry coolers, cooling towers or chillers remove heat from the building.

Efficiency and PUE

Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is total facility power divided by IT equipment power; 1.0 would be perfect. Liquid cooling can improve PUE because:

  • Pumping liquid uses less energy than moving huge volumes of air.
  • Warmer coolant temperatures allow more "free cooling" without chillers.
  • Server fans can slow down or be removed.

Leading hyperscale data centers report PUE values close to 1.1. Liquid cooling also makes waste-heat reuse practical, for example heating nearby buildings.

Water use

Liquid cooling inside the rack typically uses closed loops that do not consume water. Water consumption depends mainly on how the facility rejects heat: evaporative cooling towers use water, while dry coolers use little water but more electricity. Data center operators increasingly report water usage effectiveness and choose designs based on local climate and water scarcity. See how much energy AI uses.

Costs and deployment challenges

  • Capital cost: CDUs, plumbing and facility upgrades add upfront cost, though density gains can reduce floor space and building costs.
  • Retrofits: many existing data centers were designed for air; adding liquid cooling requires major changes to power and plumbing.
  • Operations: technicians need new skills, and leak detection and coolant quality management become essential.
  • Standardisation: industry groups such as the Open Compute Project are working on common designs.
  • Supply chain: CDUs, cold plates and fittings have seen surging demand.

What liquid cooling means for GPU availability

The newest GPUs, such as B200 and especially GB200 and future rack-scale systems, often require liquid-cooled facilities. That limits which data centers can host them and affects cloud availability and pricing. Older air-cooled GPUs like the H100 and H200 remain easier to deploy. Compare current prices in our GPU cloud price tracker and read H200 vs B200.

Liquid cooling at home

Enthusiasts use all-in-one or custom water loops for high-end GPUs like the RTX 5090, mainly to reduce noise and temperatures. For most home AI workstations, good airflow and sensible power limits are enough. See how to build an AI workstation and GPU power consumption for AI.

The future of AI cooling

  • Higher rack densities as rack-scale systems grow, possibly reaching hundreds of kilowatts or more per rack.
  • Two-phase and advanced cold plates for chips beyond 1,500 W.
  • Co-packaged optics to reduce networking power.
  • Heat reuse for district heating and industrial processes.
  • Purpose-built AI campuses designed for liquid cooling from the ground up.

Frequently asked questions

Why do AI GPUs need liquid cooling?

Because modern AI accelerators draw around 700–1,200 W each, packed densely into racks drawing 100 kW or more, which air cannot cool efficiently.

Is liquid cooling safe for electronics?

Yes, when designed properly. Direct-to-chip systems use sealed loops with leak detection, and immersion systems use non-conductive fluids.

Does liquid cooling save energy?

Usually. It reduces fan and chiller energy and enables higher coolant temperatures, improving facility efficiency.

Is the H100 liquid-cooled?

Most H100 systems are air-cooled, though liquid-cooled versions exist. Liquid cooling becomes much more common with Blackwell-generation rack-scale systems.

  • ASHRAE TC 9.9, *Thermal Guidelines for Data Processing Environments*
  • Open Compute Project (cooling environments and advanced cooling projects)
  • International Energy Agency, Energy and AI (2025)

content:
Short answer

LLM cost per token comes down to one formula: GPU cost per hour ÷ tokens generated per hour. A GPU renting for $3.92/hour (the median H100 price on our tracker) that serves 1,500 tokens per second across many users costs about $0.73 per million output tokens; the same GPU serving a single user at 50 tokens per second costs about $22 per million. The biggest levers are batching (utilisation), model size, quantization and hardware choice. APIs are usually cheaper for small or bursty workloads; self-hosting can win at high, steady volume or when privacy requires it.

The core formula

cost per 1M tokens = GPU cost per hour ÷ (tokens per second × 3,600) × 1,000,000

Two numbers drive everything:

1. What you pay per GPU-hour (cloud price, or amortised hardware plus power). 2. How many tokens that GPU produces per hour, which depends on model size, hardware, software and how many requests you batch together.

Today's GPU prices (inputs to the formula)

From the TensorCore.si GPU cloud price tracker on November 27, 2026 (on-demand, per GPU-hour):

Why throughput varies so much

Worked examples

All examples use output tokens and assume costs at median rental prices. Real throughput depends on model, engine and settings.

The lesson: utilisation matters more than almost anything else. An idle or lightly used GPU is expensive per token; a well-batched one is cheap.

Input vs output tokens

APIs usually charge less for input tokens than output tokens, because:

  • Input (prefill) is processed in parallel and uses the GPU efficiently.
  • Output (decode) is generated one token at a time and is memory-bound.

Prompt caching can reduce input costs further when the same long system prompt or documents are reused. See prefill vs decode and What are tokens in AI?.

Reasoning models change the maths

Reasoning models generate many hidden "thinking" tokens before answering. A question that needs 500 visible tokens might generate 5,000 or more in total, multiplying cost per answer. Measure cost per task, not just cost per token.

API vs self-hosting

Break-even rule of thumb: self-hosting makes sense when you can keep GPUs busy most of the time. Calculate your expected tokens per month, the equivalent API cost, and compare with GPU-hours needed at realistic utilisation.

Owning hardware: cost per token at home

For a purchased GPU, include amortised hardware and electricity:

hourly cost = (hardware price ÷ expected hours of use) + (watts ÷ 1,000 × electricity price)

Example: a $2,000 GPU used 4,000 hours over its life is $0.50/hour, plus about $0.07/hour of electricity at 450 W and $0.15/kWh. See GPU power consumption for AI and rent vs buy a GPU.

The biggest levers to cut cost

1. Batch requests with an engine that supports continuous batching. 2. Use the smallest model that meets quality needs; see small language models. 3. Quantize to FP8, FP4 or 4-bit where quality allows; see LLM quantization. 4. Use prefix caching for repeated prompts and documents. 5. Choose the right GPU: cheapest per token, not cheapest per hour; see H200 vs B200. 6. Use spot or reserved capacity for predictable workloads; see cloud GPU providers compared. 7. Limit output length and reasoning effort when not needed. 8. Route requests: send easy tasks to small models and hard ones to large models.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to run ChatGPT-like models?

It depends on model size and scale. Large providers serve enormous volumes with heavy batching and custom optimisation, achieving far lower cost per token than a single small deployment.

Is it cheaper to run an LLM locally?

For light personal use, local inference on a GPU you already own costs mainly electricity. For high-quality large models or many users, cloud GPUs or APIs are often more practical.

What is a good cost per million tokens?

It varies widely by model quality, from a few cents for small models to tens of dollars for the most capable reasoning models. Compare cost per completed task rather than raw token prices.

Why is batching so important?

Because generating a token requires reading all model weights from memory. Serving many users at once shares that cost across many tokens.

LABEL: GUIDE

EXCERPT: Two 24 GB GPUs can run a 70B model that no single consumer card can hold. A complete multi-GPU LLM setup guide: how splitting a model across GPUs works, tensor vs pipeline parallelism, configuring llama.cpp, Ollama and vLLM, PCIe lanes, NVLink, mixing different GPUs, power supplies, cooling and realistic performance expectations.
KEY: A multi-GPU LLM setup lets you combine the VRAM of several graphics cards to run models too large for one GPU. Two 24 GB cards (for example 2 × RTX 3090) give 48 GB, enough for a 70B model at 4-bit. Tools split the model in two main ways: layer splitting (pipeline style), used by default in llama.cpp and Ollama, which is simple and works with mixed GPUs; and tensor parallelism, used by vLLM, which splits each layer across GPUs for higher speed but needs matched GPUs and benefits from fast interconnects. content:
Short answer

A multi-GPU LLM setup lets you combine the VRAM of several graphics cards to run models too large for one GPU. Two 24 GB cards (for example 2 × RTX 3090) give 48 GB, enough for a 70B model at 4-bit. Tools split the model in two main ways: layer splitting (pipeline style), used by default in llama.cpp and Ollama, which is simple and works with mixed GPUs; and tensor parallelism, used by vLLM, which splits each layer across GPUs for higher speed but needs matched GPUs and benefits from fast interconnects. RTX 40 and 50 series cards have no NVLink, so GPUs communicate over PCIe. Plan for power (a 1,200–1,600 W PSU for two high-end cards), physical space and cooling.

Why use multiple GPUs?

  • More memory: the main reason. VRAM adds up across cards for holding model weights and KV cache.
  • More speed: with tensor parallelism, multiple GPUs can generate tokens faster than one.
  • More users: serve several people at once.

Multiple GPUs do not combine into one big GPU automatically; software must split the model.

How models are split across GPUs

For background, see parallelism in distributed training and NVLink explained.

Popular multi-GPU builds

Use our VRAM calculator to check fit, and see best open source LLMs to run locally.

Setting up the software

Ollama

Ollama detects multiple GPUs automatically and spreads a model's layers across them when it does not fit on one. You can restrict which GPUs it uses with:

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 ollama serve

llama.cpp

# Split layers across two GPUs in a 1:1 ratio, all layers on GPU
./llama-server -m model-70b-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 --tensor-split 1,1

# Uneven cards (e.g. 32 GB + 24 GB): split proportionally
./llama-server -m model.gguf -ngl 99 --tensor-split 32,24

# Try row split on similar GPUs
./llama-server -m model.gguf -ngl 99 --split-mode row

Key flags: -ngl (layers on GPU), --tensor-split (proportion per GPU), --split-mode layer|row, --main-gpu.

vLLM (tensor parallelism)

vllm serve <model-name> --tensor-parallel-size 2

vLLM requires the model to fit across the GPUs with room for its KV cache and works best with identical GPUs. It shines when serving multiple users thanks to continuous batching. See LLM inference engines compared.

ExLlamaV2/V3 and others

ExLlama-based tools (such as TabbyAPI) support splitting across GPUs with fast quantized formats, and LM Studio offers GPU allocation settings in its interface.

Hardware considerations

PCIe lanes and slots

For layer-split inference, PCIe bandwidth matters little once the model is loaded, because only small activations pass between GPUs per token. Tensor parallelism and training are much more sensitive. A slot wired at x4 through the chipset still works for inference but loads models more slowly.

NVLink

  • RTX 3090 supports an NVLink bridge between two cards, which can help tensor parallel performance.
  • RTX 4090 and RTX 50 series have no NVLink; communication goes over PCIe.
  • Data center GPUs (H100, B200) use NVLink and NVSwitch for very fast multi-GPU communication.

Power

Tip: power-limit each GPU (for example nvidia-smi -pl 280 on a 3090). Inference speed usually drops only slightly, while total power and heat fall substantially. Check your household circuit capacity too. See GPU power consumption for AI.

Physical space and cooling

  • Modern high-end GPUs are 3–4 slots thick. Check motherboard slot spacing and case size.
  • Blower-style or water-cooled cards are easier to stack.
  • PCIe riser cables and open-frame cases are popular for 3–4 GPU rigs.
  • Leave space between cards; the top card in a stack often runs hottest.

System RAM and CPU

Have at least as much system RAM as total VRAM (more for MoE expert offload), and a CPU with enough PCIe lanes for your GPU count. See how to build an AI workstation.

Mixing different GPUs

  • llama.cpp / Ollama: mixing works well (for example a 5090 with a 3090). Speed is limited by the slower card for its share of layers.
  • vLLM tensor parallelism: use identical GPUs.
  • Mixing generations: use a driver and CUDA version that supports all cards.
  • Mixing NVIDIA and AMD: possible with some backends (for example Vulkan in llama.cpp) but more complex.

Realistic performance expectations

Single-user token generation is limited by memory bandwidth; tensor parallelism helps because both GPUs read their half of the weights at the same time. Actual numbers vary with software, quantization and context length.

Multi-GPU vs alternatives

Also see rent vs buy a GPU and best GPU for local LLMs.

Troubleshooting

Frequently asked questions

Does adding a second GPU double speed?

Not with layer splitting, which mainly adds memory. Tensor parallelism can increase speed, but rarely by a full 2×.

Can I use two different GPUs for an LLM?

Yes, with llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio. vLLM tensor parallelism works best with identical GPUs.

Do I need NVLink for multi-GPU inference?

No. Layer-split inference works well over PCIe. NVLink helps tensor parallelism and training.

Is 2 × RTX 3090 still worth it?

For running 70B-class models on a budget, two used RTX 3090s remain one of the best-value options thanks to 48 GB total VRAM and NVLink support.

  • vLLM documentation, Parallelism and scaling
  • Shoeybi et al., Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism (2019)
  • Ollama documentation

content:
Short answer

The NVIDIA GPU roadmap has accelerated from a new data center architecture every two years to roughly one major release per year. Volta (2017) introduced tensor cores, Ampere (2020) added TF32 and BF16, Hopper (2022) brought FP8 and the Transformer Engine, Blackwell (2024–2025) added FP4 and dual-die GPUs, and Blackwell Ultra (2025) raised memory to 288 GB. NVIDIA has announced Vera Rubin for 2026 with HBM4 memory, Rubin Ultra for 2027 and Feynman after that. Each step increases AI throughput through lower precision, more memory bandwidth, faster NVLink and larger rack-scale systems. Future specifications can change, so treat announced figures as plans.

Data center GPU architectures at a glance

Turing (2018, T4 and RTX 20) and Ada Lovelace (2022, L40S and RTX 40) served inference and graphics between these generations. For tensor core details by generation, see tensor core generations and how tensor cores work.

Generation by generation

Volta (2017): the tensor core arrives

The V100 introduced the first tensor cores, accelerating FP16 matrix maths for deep learning and launching NVIDIA's dominance in AI training.

Ampere (2020): the AI workhorse

The A100 added TF32 (FP32-range math with tensor core speed), BF16, 2:4 structured sparsity and Multi-Instance GPU partitioning. It powered the training of GPT-3-era models and remains widely rented. See H100 vs A100.

Hopper (2022–2024): built for transformers

The H100 introduced FP8 with the Transformer Engine, the Tensor Memory Accelerator, asynchronous warpgroup matrix instructions and NVLink 4. It became the defining GPU of the generative AI boom. The H200 kept the same chip but upgraded to 141 GB of HBM3e. See H100 vs H200 and H100 PCIe vs SXM.

Blackwell (2024–2025): two dies, FP4 and rack-scale

Blackwell joins two reticle-sized dies into one GPU, adds FP4 and FP6 support with micro-scaled formats such as NVFP4, doubles NVLink bandwidth and introduced the GB200 NVL72, a liquid-cooled rack where 72 GPUs act as one NVLink domain. See Hopper vs Blackwell, B200 vs H100, H200 vs B200 and GB200 NVL72 explained.

Blackwell Ultra (2025): more memory and inference speed

The B300 and GB300 increase memory to 288 GB of HBM3e and boost FP4 compute and attention performance, targeting reasoning-model inference. See B200 vs B300.

Vera Rubin (2026): HBM4 and the Vera CPU

NVIDIA announced Rubin as Blackwell's successor, pairing Rubin GPUs with its custom Arm-based Vera CPU, using HBM4 memory and next-generation NVLink in larger rack-scale systems. NVIDIA also announced Rubin CPX, a specialised accelerator for the compute-heavy context (prefill) phase of long-context inference. See NVIDIA Rubin explained and What is HBM4?.

Rubin Ultra (2027) and Feynman (2028)

NVIDIA's roadmap shows Rubin Ultra with larger multi-die GPUs and much larger NVLink racks, followed by an architecture named after physicist Richard Feynman. Details will be revealed closer to launch.

The trends behind the roadmap

Consumer and workstation GPUs

TITLE: Superintelligence and Human Enhancement: Can Brain-Computer Interfaces Help Us Keep Up?
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
META: Superintelligence and human enhancement: can brain-computer interfaces like Neuralink, cognitive enhancement or merging with AI help humans keep up?
EXCERPT: Some technologists argue humans must merge with AI to stay relevant in a world of superintelligence. A deep look at brain-computer interfaces (Neuralink, Synchron, BrainGate), the bandwidth problem, cognitive and genetic enhancement, AI-augmented humans, and the ethical, safety and inequality questions they raise.

content:
Short answer

Superintelligence and human enhancement are often discussed together. The idea that humans could keep pace with superintelligence by merging with AI is popular among some technologists, most famously Elon Musk, whose company Neuralink implanted its first human patient in 2024. Today's brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are genuine medical breakthroughs, letting paralysed people control computers and even speak through decoded neural signals. But the brain-computer interface superintelligence vision faces a huge gap: current BCIs transmit far less information than the brain processes, and adding bandwidth does not make the brain itself faster. In the near term, the most powerful form of "enhancement" is simply humans working closely with AI tools.

Why people talk about merging with AI

If AI becomes far more capable than humans, one fear is that humans become irrelevant or lose control. A proposed solution: connect brains directly to AI, so humans share in its capabilities rather than competing with them. This connects to debates about what happens after superintelligence and meaning in a world with SI.

What brain-computer interfaces can do today

These are remarkable medical advances that restore lost abilities. They are not yet enhancements for healthy people.

The bandwidth problem

Researchers have estimated that spoken languages convey information at a similar rate of roughly 39 bits per second, regardless of language. The brain's output is slow compared with computers. Even a perfect BCI that removed the keyboard bottleneck would not make human thinking faster: the limit is how fast our neurons process ideas, not how fast we type. That is the core challenge for the "merge" vision. Compare with GPU memory bandwidth.

Paths to human enhancement

1. AI-augmented humans (already happening)

The most practical enhancement today is external: humans using AI assistants, AI agents and tools that extend memory, analysis and creativity. A person with a superintelligent assistant could achieve far more than any unaided expert.

2. High-bandwidth BCIs

Future devices with many more electrodes, better decoding and wireless power could allow richer two-way communication: controlling complex software by thought, receiving sensory information or perhaps sharing concepts with AI systems. Writing information into the brain (not just reading it) remains far more difficult.

3. Cognitive enhancement drugs and stimulation

So-called nootropics and brain stimulation have shown modest effects at best in healthy people. No current method dramatically increases general intelligence.

4. Genetic enhancement

Intelligence is partly heritable and influenced by thousands of genetic variants, each with tiny effects. Embryo screening for polygenic scores is offered commercially in some countries but is scientifically and ethically controversial, and its predictive power for individuals is limited. Gene editing for intelligence is not feasible today and raises profound ethical questions. Even optimistic scenarios would take generations, far slower than AI progress.

5. Mind uploading and brain emulation

Scanning and simulating a human brain digitally is discussed as a long-term path, but brain mapping has only recently reached a complete fruit fly brain (about 140,000 neurons) and a cubic millimetre of mouse cortex. A human brain has about 86 billion neurons. See how we could achieve superintelligence.

Comparing enhancement paths

Ethical and social questions

  • Safety: brain surgery carries risks; long-term effects of implants are still being studied.
  • Privacy: neural data is the most intimate data imaginable. Several places have begun passing "neurorights" or neural-data protection laws.
  • Security: a connected brain device could be hacked.
  • Autonomy: who controls the AI connected to your brain, and could it influence your thoughts or choices?
  • Inequality: if enhancement is expensive, it could create biological class divides.
  • Identity: at what point does a merged human-AI stop being the same person?
  • Consent: especially for genetic choices affecting future generations.

Does merging solve the superintelligence problem?

Supporters argue that keeping humans "in the loop" at a neural level could keep AI aligned with human interests. Critics raise three points:

1. Timing: AI is advancing far faster than neurotechnology. 2. The weak link: if a superintelligence is connected to a human brain, the brain is still the slowest and least capable part, so the AI's goals and design would still dominate. 3. Alignment still required: connecting to a misaligned system does not make it aligned; it could make humans more vulnerable to influence.

Most alignment researchers therefore focus on making AI itself safe. See the superintelligence control problem and AI alignment.

What is realistic in the coming years

  • BCIs will improve rapidly as medical devices, restoring movement and speech for people with paralysis and other conditions.
  • Non-invasive wearables may offer simple control inputs.
  • The biggest boost for most people will come from AI tools, not implants.
  • Debates about neural data rights will grow.

Frequently asked questions

Can Neuralink make people smarter?

Not today. Neuralink's current trials focus on helping people with paralysis control devices. There is no evidence that implants increase intelligence.

Will humans merge with AI?

Some people will use increasingly intimate interfaces, but a full merger of human minds with superintelligence is speculative and faces large scientific and ethical hurdles.

Is it possible to upload a mind to a computer?

Not with current technology. It would require mapping and simulating the human brain in extraordinary detail, far beyond today's capabilities.

Are brain-computer interfaces safe?

Implanted BCIs involve surgery and are tested under strict medical oversight. Long-term safety is still being studied.

  • Card et al., An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis (New England Journal of Medicine, 2024)
  • BrainGate, BrainGate research consortium
  • Dorkenwald et al., Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain (Nature, 2024)
  • Bostrom, *Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies* (Oxford University Press, 2014)

LABEL: DEEP DIVE
META: Superintelligence and medicine: how SI could design drugs, diagnose disease, slow ageing and transform healthcare, plus the evidence, bottlenecks and risks.

KEY: Superintelligence and medicine may be the most hopeful pairing in the AI debate. Early signs are real: AlphaFold predicted structures for hundreds of millions of proteins and won a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and AI-designed drugs have reached mid-stage clinical trials. content:
Short answer

Superintelligence and medicine may be the most hopeful pairing in the AI debate. A superintelligence could read every biomedical paper, model cells and proteins, design drug candidates in days, diagnose disease better than specialists and personalise treatment to each genome. Early signs are real: AlphaFold predicted structures for hundreds of millions of proteins and won a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and AI-designed drugs have reached mid-stage clinical trials. But medicine is constrained by biology's complexity, the time needed to test treatments in people, regulation and access. SI could compress decades of progress into years; it is unlikely to deliver instant cures for everything.

Why medicine is a natural fit for superintelligence

Biomedicine has three properties that suit superhuman intelligence:

1. Too much knowledge for any human. Millions of papers are published every year; no doctor or scientist can read even a fraction. 2. Enormous search spaces. The number of possible drug-like molecules is astronomically large, far beyond what human chemists can explore. 3. Complex systems. Diseases emerge from interactions between genes, proteins, cells, organs and environment, ideal for systems that can hold many variables at once.

What today's AI has already achieved

See AI scientists and discovery and computer vision for related advances.

What superintelligence could do in medicine

1. Drug discovery and design

  • Identify disease targets by integrating genetics, protein data and clinical records.
  • Design molecules optimised for potency, safety, absorption and manufacturability simultaneously.
  • Predict toxicity and side effects before synthesis, eliminating many failures early.
  • Design biologics: antibodies, enzymes, gene therapies and vaccines.
  • Repurpose existing approved drugs for new diseases quickly.

Today, developing a new drug typically takes over a decade, and the large majority of candidates entering clinical trials fail. Even modest improvements in predicting failure would save years and billions.

2. Diagnosis and clinical care

  • Expert-level diagnosis from symptoms, images, lab results and genomes, available anywhere.
  • Earlier detection of cancer, heart disease and neurodegeneration from subtle patterns.
  • Continuous monitoring through wearables, flagging problems before symptoms appear.
  • Treatment plans that weigh every patient's history, medications and preferences.

3. Personalised and precision medicine

Every patient's genome, microbiome and biology differ. SI could predict how each individual will respond to a drug and dose, design personalised cancer vaccines based on a tumour's mutations, and model a "digital twin" of a patient to test treatments virtually.

4. Ageing and longevity

Ageing is the main risk factor for most chronic diseases. Researchers already study interventions that extend healthy lifespan in animals. A superintelligence might untangle the biology of ageing (cellular senescence, epigenetic changes, mitochondrial decline) and propose interventions. This is the most speculative area: any claim that SI will "cure ageing" goes well beyond current evidence.

5. Global health

Low-cost expert diagnosis, optimised supply chains, epidemic forecasting and vaccine design could save the most lives in places with the fewest doctors. Translation and guidance in local languages could bring expert-level care to billions.

6. Mental health

AI tools could expand access to evidence-based support, though human care, safety and trust remain essential. Superintelligent systems would need careful design to help rather than harm vulnerable people.

The bottlenecks: why SI won't cure everything overnight

These limits echo the broader point in what superintelligence could do and its limits: intelligence accelerates thinking, but the physical world sets the pace of experiments.

The risks

  • Biosecurity: the same capabilities that design medicines could help design harmful pathogens. Frontier labs and governments test models for biological misuse risks and restrict dangerous capabilities. This is one of the most serious concerns about advanced AI.
  • Errors at scale: a flawed AI model deployed across millions of patients could cause widespread harm.
  • Bias: models trained on unrepresentative data may perform worse for some groups.
  • Privacy: health data is among the most sensitive personal information.
  • Over-reliance: clinicians might defer to AI even when it is wrong.
  • Inequality: breakthroughs could be available only to the wealthy.

See positive and negative impacts of superintelligence and AI alignment.

A realistic timeline of change

Hardware behind medical AI

Protein-structure prediction, molecular simulation and medical multimodal models run on data center GPUs and TPUs. Training large biology foundation models uses the same clusters as language models. See how much compute superintelligence needs and our GPU cloud price tracker.

Frequently asked questions

Will superintelligence cure cancer?

It could greatly accelerate progress against many cancers through better targets, drugs and personalised treatments. "Cancer" is hundreds of different diseases, and every treatment still needs testing, so progress would likely be uneven rather than a single cure.

Could superintelligence make people live forever?

There is no evidence that indefinite lifespan is achievable. SI might significantly extend healthy lifespan if ageing biology proves tractable, but this is speculative.

Will AI replace doctors?

AI will take over many diagnostic and administrative tasks, but patients value human care, judgement and accountability. See which jobs superintelligence will affect.

Is AI-designed medicine safe?

AI-designed drugs go through the same clinical trials and regulatory review as any other medicine.

  • Abramson et al., Accurate structure prediction of biomolecular interactions with AlphaFold 3 (Nature, 2024)
  • The Nobel Prize, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024

  • Amodei, Machines of Loving Grace (2024)

content:
Short answer

What is the meaning of life after superintelligence? The hardest question about superintelligence may not be technical but personal: what gives life meaning when machines can do almost everything better than we can? Psychology suggests meaning comes less from being the best and more from autonomy, competence, relationships and contributing to something larger. History offers hope: chess became more popular after computers surpassed grandmasters. The meaning of life after superintelligence is likely to shift from productive work toward relationships, craft, play, exploration, care and spiritual life, but that transition will need deliberate support from societies, not just abundance.

Why this question matters now

For most of history, work has provided income, structure, identity, social connection and status. Superintelligence could automate much of that work. Even in a world of material abundance, people could face a crisis of purpose. Philosophers and economists have anticipated this:

  • John Maynard Keynes (1930) predicted that his grandchildren's generation might work 15 hours a week and face "man's permanent problem": how to occupy the leisure that science would win.
  • Nick Bostrom's *Deep Utopia* (2024) explores what meaning could look like in a "solved world" where technology removes the need for human effort.

Where meaning comes from: what psychology says

The key insight: meaning rarely depends on being the best in the world. Amateur musicians, weekend runners and gardeners find deep satisfaction without competing with professionals.

Lessons from history

Chess after Deep Blue

When IBM's Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997, some predicted the end of chess. Instead, chess became more popular than ever, especially with online play and streaming. Computers became training partners and analysis tools. People still watch humans play because human drama, struggle and personality matter.

The aristocracy and leisure classes

Throughout history, some groups lived without needing to work. Some found purpose in arts, science, politics, sport and philanthropy; others suffered boredom and decadence. Abundance did not automatically create meaning; culture and expectations did.

Retirement and unemployment research

Studies of retirees and long-term unemployed people show that losing work can harm wellbeing, mainly through loss of structure, social contact, identity and income. Retirees who replace these with community roles, hobbies, volunteering and relationships often thrive. This is a clue for a post-work society.

Where people might find meaning after SI

1. Relationships and care

Human connection is the most consistent predictor of wellbeing in happiness research. With more time, people could invest in family, friendships and communities. Caring for children, elders and each other would remain deeply human, even if AI assists.

2. Craft and mastery

People will still bake bread, build furniture, play instruments and learn languages, not because machines can't, but because the process itself is satisfying. "Human-made" may gain value, as handmade goods did after industrialisation.

3. Play, sport and games

Games are voluntary challenges; their value doesn't depend on being useful. Sport, games and adventures could become central to human life.

4. Exploration and learning

With superintelligent tutors, people could learn anything for its own sake. Travel, discovery and, perhaps eventually, space exploration offer purpose. See what superintelligence could do.

5. Art and expression

AI can generate art, but human art expresses a particular person's experience. Audiences may value the human story behind a work, as they value live performance over recordings.

6. Community, politics and governance

Deciding how society uses superintelligence, what values it serves and how benefits are shared, is a profoundly human responsibility. Civic life could become more important, not less. See superintelligence geopolitics.

7. Spiritual and philosophical life

Religious and philosophical traditions have long taught that human worth does not depend on productivity. Many may find renewed relevance in a world where people must define value beyond economic usefulness.

The risks to meaning

What societies can do

1. Share the gains: material security is a precondition for meaning. See the economics of superintelligence. 2. Invest in community infrastructure: parks, libraries, clubs, sports, arts centres and volunteering. 3. Redesign education: teach curiosity, relationships, ethics, creativity and self-direction, not only job skills. 4. Protect human agency: keep important decisions under human control. 5. Honour non-economic contribution: care work, volunteering and community leadership. 6. Encourage healthy AI design: systems that support wellbeing rather than maximise screen time.

What individuals can do now

  • Build relationships that don't depend on work.
  • Develop hobbies and skills you value for their own sake.
  • Practise using AI as a tool for growth, not a replacement for effort you care about.
  • Engage in your community and in debates about how AI should be governed.
  • Reflect on your values: what would you do if you didn't need to work?

Frequently asked questions

Will humans become useless if superintelligence arrives?

Economically, much human labour may become unnecessary. But human worth has never been only economic. People can matter to each other, create, care, explore and decide together.

Will people still work after superintelligence?

Probably, but more by choice: in roles where people want human involvement, in creative pursuits, and in caring and community work. See which jobs superintelligence will affect.

Could superintelligence help us find meaning?

It could help by providing time, security and personalised learning, and by helping people reflect. It should not decide what is meaningful for us.

Is a world without work a good world?

It depends on whether people have security, agency, relationships and opportunities for purpose. History shows leisure can be fulfilling or empty depending on culture and support.

Sources and further reading

  • Keynes, Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren (1930)
  • Bostrom, *Deep Utopia: Life and Meaning in a Solved World* (Ideapress, 2024)
  • Ryan and Deci, "Self-Determination Theory and the Facilitation of Intrinsic Motivation, Social Development, and Well-Being", *American Psychologist* (2000)
  • Csikszentmihalyi, *Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience* (Harper & Row, 1990)
  • Frankl, *Man's Search for Meaning* (1946)

EXCERPT: Could superintelligence do the work of millions of scientists? An in-depth look at AI scientific discovery today (AlphaFold, GNoME, AlphaEvolve, AI co-scientists, self-driving labs), the stages of automating science, what superintelligence could add, and the bottlenecks of experiments, verification and trust.
KEY: AI scientific discovery has moved from tools that help scientists to systems that generate hypotheses, run experiments and find genuinely new results. AlphaFold transformed protein science; GNoME proposed hundreds of thousands of potentially stable new materials; AlphaEvolve improved a decades-old algorithm for multiplying matrices; and "AI scientist" systems now draft papers and propose testable ideas. content:
Short answer

AI scientific discovery has moved from tools that help scientists to systems that generate hypotheses, run experiments and find genuinely new results. AlphaFold transformed protein science; GNoME proposed hundreds of thousands of potentially stable new materials; AlphaEvolve improved a decades-old algorithm for multiplying matrices; and "AI scientist" systems now draft papers and propose testable ideas. A superintelligence could run this process at enormous scale, effectively adding millions of tireless researchers. The limits are experiment throughput, verification and trust: discoveries still need real-world testing, and humans must be able to check them.

Why science is the key to everything else

Most of the benefits people hope for from superintelligence, such as cures, clean energy, new materials and space travel, come through scientific discovery. Science is also the route by which AI could improve AI itself. That makes AI-driven discovery one of the most important topics in understanding how superintelligence could be achieved and what it could do.

How science works, and which parts AI can do

Milestones in AI-driven discovery

Four levels of AI in science

1. AI as a tool: prediction models used by humans, like AlphaFold. Humans ask the questions. 2. AI as an assistant: language models read papers, write code and analyse data on request. 3. AI as a collaborator: systems propose hypotheses and experiments; humans choose and validate. This is where AI co-scientists sit today. 4. AI as an autonomous scientist: systems set research agendas, run experiments through robotic labs and publish verified results. This is where superintelligence would operate.

The jump from level 3 to level 4 is the heart of the intelligence explosion argument when the science in question is AI research itself.

What superintelligence could add

  • Scale: millions of parallel research threads, each as capable as a top scientist. See how much compute superintelligence needs.
  • Breadth: connecting results across physics, chemistry, biology and engineering that no human specialist would link.
  • Speed: turning around hypothesis, simulation and analysis in minutes.
  • Memory: never forgetting a negative result, a failed experiment or an obscure paper.
  • New mathematics: developing theoretical frameworks and proofs, checked by formal proof assistants.
  • Better experiments: designing each experiment to be maximally informative, cutting the number needed.

Possible high-impact areas: materials for batteries and superconductors, catalysts for clean fuels, fusion plasma control, protein and enzyme design, climate modelling, chip design and medicine (see superintelligence and medicine).

The bottlenecks

1. Experiment throughput

Thinking is fast; reality is slow. Growing cells, synthesising compounds, building prototypes and running clinical trials take time and physical resources. Self-driving labs help, but scaling them requires investment, robotics and materials. Economists call this the physical bottleneck, discussed in the economics of superintelligence.

2. Verification

If an AI produces a 300-page proof or a new physical theory, how do humans check it? Formal verification works for mathematics; for empirical science, independent replication remains essential. This connects to scalable oversight.

3. Data quality

Much scientific literature is irreproducible or biased toward positive results. An AI trained on flawed data may inherit errors. Generating new, high-quality data through experiments becomes crucial.

4. Hallucination and overconfidence

AI systems can generate plausible but wrong claims, citations or results. See AI hallucinations. Scientific AI needs rigorous checking, especially when results guide expensive experiments.

5. Reward hacking

Systems optimised to produce "successful" papers or passing tests may exploit loopholes rather than discover real truths. See early warning signs in today's AI.

6. Dual-use risks

Some knowledge, especially in biology and chemistry, can cause great harm. Safeguards and governance are needed for AI-driven research in sensitive areas.

How human scientists' roles may change

Science may become more like directing a vast research organisation, with humans setting goals, values and priorities. See which jobs superintelligence will affect.

How to tell real AI discoveries from hype

1. Has the result been independently verified or replicated? 2. Was it published in a peer-reviewed venue or formally proven? 3. Is the AI's contribution clearly separated from human input? 4. Does the discovery hold up in real experiments, not only simulations? 5. Are failures and limitations reported honestly?

Frequently asked questions

Has AI made a real scientific discovery?

Yes. AlphaFold's protein structures, new mathematical constructions from FunSearch and AlphaEvolve, and AI-proposed materials and hypotheses later confirmed in labs are genuine contributions, though most still involve human direction and validation.

Will AI win a Nobel Prize?

Nobel Prizes go to people. In 2024, the Chemistry prize recognised the scientists behind AlphaFold, and the Physics prize honoured foundational work on neural networks.

Could superintelligence solve physics?

It could greatly speed progress, but fundamental physics needs experiments, some requiring huge facilities such as particle colliders and telescopes. Theory alone cannot settle every question.

Is AI-generated science trustworthy?

Only after verification. Treat AI-generated results like any new claim: check methods, replication and evidence.

  • Lu et al., The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery (2024)
  • Gottweis et al., Towards an AI co-scientist (Google, 2025)
  • Google DeepMind, AlphaEvolve (2025)
  • Romera-Paredes et al., Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models (FunSearch, Nature, 2023)
